claim: Before the user types anything, Claude Code has already loaded CLAUDE.md, auto memory, MCP tool names and skill descriptions into context, so these form the fixed session-start cost.
why: The context-window page lists these as the startup load, with output styles and --append-system-prompt text as possible additions.
check: Run /context in a real session and sum the startup categories; a large fixed total from instructions, MCP names and skill descriptions is the baseline cost every message carries.
quote: CLAUDE.md, auto memory, MCP tool names, and skill descriptions all load into context.

claim: After compaction, invoked skill bodies are re-injected but capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens in total, with the oldest invoked skills dropped first.
why: The caps bound how much skill text can survive a compaction.
check: Look for skills longer than about 5,000 tokens or workflows that invoke many skills in one session; their tails or older members will be lost after compaction.
quote: Re-injected, capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens total; oldest dropped first

claim: Truncation of an oversized skill after compaction keeps the start of the file, so the most important instructions belong at the top of SKILL.md.
why: Large skills are cut to fit the per-skill cap and only the beginning survives.
check: Check that critical rules in long SKILL.md files appear near the top, not buried at the end.
quote: Truncation keeps the start of the file, so put the most important instructions near the top of `SKILL.md`.

claim: After compaction Claude Code re-reads at most five previously read or edited files, most recently modified first, and any of them over 5,000 tokens comes back only as a path reference.
why: Re-reading is budgeted so compaction does not refill the window.
check: Do not rely on file contents surviving compaction; a workflow that needs large files after compaction must re-read them deliberately.
quote: A file over 5,000 tokens comes back as a path reference without its content, shown as `Referenced file` instead of `Read`.

claim: Path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md files enter message history when triggered, so compaction summarizes them away; a rule that must persist should drop its paths frontmatter or live in the project-root CLAUDE.md.
why: Only project-root CLAUDE.md and unscoped rules are re-injected from disk; the others reload on demand.
check: Find must-always-hold rules placed in paths-scoped rule files or nested CLAUDE.md; they may vanish after compaction until a matching file is touched again.
quote: Path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md files load into message history when Claude reads, writes, or edits their trigger file, so compaction summarizes them away with everything else.

claim: Context that hooks added earlier in a session is summarized with the rest of the conversation at compaction, while SessionStart hooks matching the compact source re-run and add their output to the compacted context.
why: Hook output is ordinary conversation content unless a SessionStart hook re-injects it.
check: If a hook injects context that must persist, verify it has a SessionStart hook matching compact rather than relying on a one-time injection.
quote: Claude Code runs them and adds their output to the compacted context

claim: /context gives a live per-category breakdown of context usage with optimization suggestions and shows which CLAUDE.md and auto memory files loaded; /memory opens those files.
why: The page's own visualization uses representative numbers, so /context is the way to measure a real session.
check: Measure a setup's fixed cost by running /context at session start rather than estimating from file sizes.
quote: run `/context` for a live breakdown by category with optimization suggestions, including which CLAUDE.md and auto memory files loaded.

claim: Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token context window in Claude Code, and compaction works the same way at the larger limit.
why: A larger window is the option when a smaller conversation is not enough.
check: Check whether a setup selects a [1m] variant where long sessions need it and whether it assumes a 200K window elsewhere.
quote: Fable models, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5, Opus 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 4.6 support a 1 million token context window.

claim: Anthropic recommends running /clear when switching to unrelated work, because stale conversation crowds out needed files and costs tokens on every subsequent message.
why: The whole conversation is resent each request, so leftover context is paid for repeatedly.
check: Look for long-lived sessions spanning unrelated tasks and workflows that never clear.
quote: Old conversation crowds out the files you need next and costs tokens on every message.

claim: Auto memory loads only the first 200 lines or first 25KB of MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, at the start of every conversation; anything beyond that is not loaded at session start.
why: MEMORY.md is an index meant to stay short, with detail in topic files.
check: Check the size of MEMORY.md in the project memory directory; content past line 200 or 25KB is silently unavailable.
quote: The first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md`, or the first 25KB, whichever comes first, are loaded at the start of every conversation.

claim: Auto memory topic files are not loaded at startup; Claude reads them on demand with its file tools, so only the MEMORY.md index is a fixed cost.
why: Keeping detail in topic files keeps the startup load small.
check: Verify the index points to topic files rather than holding the detail itself.
quote: Claude Code doesn't load topic files such as `user_role.md` or `feedback_testing.md` at startup.

claim: Anthropic's size target for a CLAUDE.md file is under 200 lines, because longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.
why: The source ties file length to both token cost and instruction-following.
check: Count lines in every CLAUDE.md, rules file and import; files above 200 lines are a finding, as is a startup or /status warning.
quote: target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.

claim: Splitting CLAUDE.md with @path imports organizes it but does not reduce context cost, because imported files load together with the importing file.
why: Imports are expanded into context at load time.
check: Do not credit a CLAUDE.md that is small only because it imports large files; count the imported text too.
quote: help you organize a long file but don't reduce its context cost, because imported files load together with the CLAUDE.md that imports them.

claim: CLAUDE.md @imports can nest to a maximum depth of four hops.
why: Recursion is bounded.
check: Check import chains deeper than four levels; deeper files will not load.
quote: Imported files can recursively import other files, with a maximum depth of four hops.

claim: Claude Code skips a launch-loaded CLAUDE.md over 4 MiB entirely and loads none of it.
why: The hard limit is far above the 200-line recommendation but loses everything rather than truncating.
check: Flag any instruction file approaching 4 MiB, which would load nothing.
quote: Claude Code skips a file over 4 MiB and loads none of it.

claim: On-demand instruction files (subdirectory CLAUDE.md, subdirectory rules, path-scoped rules) are truncated to their start above a per-file limit of 40,000 characters on a 200K window, or 150,000 characters on 1M windows for models later than Opus 4.6/Sonnet 4.6 (200,000 for those two).
why: Claude receives only the start plus a note to read the rest, so later instructions are absent until it chooses to read them.
check: Run wc -m on nested CLAUDE.md and rules files and compare with the limit for the session's window.
quote: **1M context window**: 200,000 characters on Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, and 150,000 characters on later models

claim: CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md in the working directory and every parent directory load at launch, ordered root-down so the file nearest the working directory is read last, while those in subdirectories load only when Claude reads, writes or edits a file there.
why: Ancestor files are concatenated rather than overriding; subdirectory files are lazy.
check: In a monorepo, check which ancestor CLAUDE.md files load at launch and whether claudeMdExcludes is needed to skip other teams' files.
quote: Instead of loading them at launch, Claude Code loads each one once Claude reads, writes, or edits another file in that subdirectory.

claim: Block-level HTML comments in CLAUDE.md are stripped before injection, so maintainer notes cost no context tokens.
why: Comments inside code blocks are preserved, but ordinary block comments are removed.
check: Maintainer notes written as visible prose in CLAUDE.md are avoidable cost; they could be HTML comments.
quote: Block-level HTML comments (`<!-- maintainer notes -->`) in CLAUDE.md files are stripped before the content is injected

claim: Unscoped rules in .claude/rules load every session, whereas path-scoped rules and skills load only on matching files or when relevant; task-specific instructions belong in skills.
why: Rules load into context every session or when matching files are opened, while skills load when invoked or judged relevant.
check: Find rules files without paths frontmatter whose content applies to one task or area; they are fixed cost that could be path-scoped or become skills.
quote: Rules load into context every session or when matching files are opened.

claim: CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt rather than as part of the system prompt, and carries no guarantee of strict compliance.
why: Claude treats it as context, not enforced configuration; hooks or permissions are the enforcement path.
check: Flag rules in CLAUDE.md that must be enforced (blocking commands, mandatory steps) and should be hooks or permission rules.
quote: CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself.

claim: Claude Code warns at startup and in /status when an instruction file exceeds the recommended length, and warns again when files individually within it add up past a combined limit; each CLAUDE.md, rules file and @import counts separately.
why: The harness itself measures instruction size.
check: Ask for the /status output or startup warnings as direct evidence of oversized instruction files.
quote: If one of your instruction files is over the recommended length, you see a warning at startup and when you run `/status`.

claim: /doctor prompt-audit (Claude Code v2.1.283 or later) audits CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, AGENTS.md and the rules, skills, commands, subagents and output styles under .claude/ for outdated, missing-reference or contradictory content and proposes edits without applying them.
why: Stale instructions written for older models and conflicting files reduce adherence and waste context.
check: Run or recommend /doctor prompt-audit as a first pass on instruction files.
quote: run `/doctor prompt-audit` in a session.

claim: By default Claude reads AGENTS.md only when no CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md exists in the working directory or above, so adding a CLAUDE.local.md silently stops AGENTS.md from loading unless Project instructions is set to claude-md-and-agents-md.
why: Any project-path CLAUDE.md counts as the instruction file and displaces AGENTS.md.
check: In repos with AGENTS.md, check for a stray CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md that hides it, or for a CLAUDE.md that just says to read AGENTS.md.
quote: By default, Claude reads `AGENTS.md` only when you have no `CLAUDE.md` in your working directory or above it.

claim: A SessionStart hook that prints AGENTS.md duplicates it once Claude reads AGENTS.md natively, and should be removed.
why: The same file would be in context twice.
check: Look for SessionStart hooks that cat instruction files already loaded by the harness.
quote: Once Claude reads `AGENTS.md` directly, the hook adds a second copy to the context.

claim: CLAUDE.md files from directories added with --add-dir are not loaded unless CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD is set.
why: Extra directories grant file access but not instruction loading by default.
check: If a setup uses --add-dir and expects shared instructions, check the environment variable is set.
quote: By default, CLAUDE.md files from these directories are not loaded.

claim: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade (context rot), so what is in context matters as much as how much room is available.
why: Anthropic states a larger window is not automatically better.
check: Do not treat a 1M window as permission for bloated always-loaded context; judge each loaded piece by value.
quote: As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as *context rot*.

claim: Prompt caching changes what cached tokens cost, not whether they occupy the context window.
why: Cached prefixes still count toward the window limit.
check: Do not argue that a cached large prefix is free of context pressure; it still fills the window and affects recall.
quote: changes what you pay for those tokens, not whether they count.

claim: Everything in a request counts toward the context window: system prompt, all messages including tool results, images and documents, and tool definitions, plus the output including thinking.
why: The window is working memory for the whole request, not only conversation text.
check: Include tool definitions and system prompt when estimating a setup's fixed cost.
quote: Everything in the request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, every message in `messages` (including tool results, images, and documents), and your tool definitions.

claim: On Claude Haiku 5.5 prompts over 100,000 tokens are billed at a higher rate, the exception to standard long-context pricing on 1M-window models.
why: Other 1M-window models bill long-context requests at standard pricing.
check: For setups using Haiku 5.5 for long sessions or subagents, check whether prompts regularly pass 100,000 tokens.
quote: except on Claude Haiku 5.5, where prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more.

claim: On Opus 4.5 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later, Haiku 5.5, Fable and Mythos models the API keeps previous thinking blocks by default and they count toward the context window; earlier models strip them.
why: Retained thinking is input on later turns.
check: When estimating context growth on newer models, include accumulated thinking blocks.
quote: The API keeps previous thinking blocks by default on these models, where those blocks count toward the context window like any other input tokens:

claim: Anthropic's guiding principle for context is the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximizes the likelihood of the desired outcome.
why: Attention is a finite budget that each added token depletes.
check: Judge each always-loaded piece (instructions, tool descriptions, examples) by whether it is high-signal; a laundry list of edge cases is a finding.
quote: good context engineering means finding the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome.

claim: Anthropic says waiting for bigger windows is not a fix, since windows of all sizes suffer context pollution and relevance problems when peak agent performance is wanted.
why: It recommends compaction, note-taking and subagents instead.
check: Challenge setups that justify large always-on context by pointing at a 1M window.
quote: context windows of all sizes will be subject to context pollution and information relevance concerns

claim: Claude Code uses a hybrid context strategy: CLAUDE.md files are dropped into context up front, while glob and grep retrieve files just in time.
why: Up-front data gives speed and just-in-time retrieval avoids stale indexes.
check: Keep CLAUDE.md to what must always be known; discoverable information should be left to just-in-time retrieval.
quote: CLAUDE.md files are naively dropped into context up front, while primitives like glob and grep allow it to navigate its environment and retrieve files just-in-time

claim: Compaction is described as typically the first lever for long-horizon coherence, and tool result clearing as one of the safest, lightest-touch forms of it.
why: Raw tool results deep in history rarely need to be seen again.
check: For long agent sessions, check that some compaction or clearing strategy exists before heavier architectures are proposed.
quote: Compaction typically serves as the first lever in context engineering to drive better long-term coherence.

claim: Overly aggressive compaction can drop subtle context whose importance only appears later, so compaction prompts should first maximize recall and then improve precision.
why: What to keep versus discard is the core difficulty.
check: If a setup customizes compaction instructions, check they preserve decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details.
quote: overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later.

claim: Subagents can explore with tens of thousands of tokens but should return only a condensed summary, often 1,000-2,000 tokens, keeping the lead agent's context clean.
why: Detailed search context stays isolated in the subagent.
check: Check subagent definitions for output instructions asking for compact summaries; verbose returns defeat the isolation.
quote: returns only a condensed, distilled summary of its work (often 1,000-2,000 tokens).

claim: Anthropic names bloated tool sets with overlapping functionality or ambiguous choices as one of the most common failure modes in agent context.
why: If a human cannot say which tool applies, an agent will not do better.
check: Look for overlapping MCP servers or tools with unclear boundaries and propose pruning.
quote: One of the most common failure modes we see is bloated tool sets that cover too much functionality or lead to ambiguous decision points about which tool to use.

claim: Anthropic advises curating a few diverse canonical examples rather than stuffing a prompt with a laundry list of edge cases.
why: Examples act as pictures worth a thousand words; edge-case lists bloat the prompt.
check: Flag instruction files that enumerate dozens of edge-case rules where a few examples would do.
quote: curate a set of diverse, canonical examples that effectively portray the expected behavior of the agent

claim: Claude Code re-sends the full context every request and caches by exact prefix match, so a change anywhere in the prefix recomputes everything after it and there is no per-file caching.
why: The model keeps no memory between requests.
check: Any setup element that changes early in the request (system prompt, tool set) costs more than one that changes late.
quote: The match is exact, so a change anywhere in the prefix recomputes everything after it. There is no per-file or per-segment caching.

claim: Claude Code orders requests as system prompt (core instructions, tool definitions), then project context (CLAUDE.md, auto memory, unscoped rules), then conversation; project context changes only at session start, /clear or /compact.
why: Rarely changing content goes first to maximize prefix hits.
check: Instructions that change often belong late in the conversation, not in project context.
quote: To get the most out of prefix matching, Claude Code orders each request so content that rarely changes between turns comes first:

claim: Each model has its own cache, so switching models mid-session recomputes the whole request even if content is identical; opusplan makes every plan-mode toggle a model switch.
why: Caches are model-scoped.
check: Look for opusplan use, skills or commands that set a model in frontmatter, and habits of switching models mid-task.
quote: each model has its own cache. Switching models recomputes the entire request even when the content is identical.

claim: A skill or command whose frontmatter names a model other than the session model makes that turn a model switch, reading the whole history with no cache hits.
why: Model switching invalidates the cache.
check: Check skills with a model frontmatter field on long sessions; each invocation costs an uncached read.
quote: that turn is also a model switch: the next request reads the entire conversation history with no cache hits.

claim: On most models each effort level has its own cache, so changing effort mid-session recomputes the whole request; with an API key or subscription the cache stays intact on Fable 5.1 and later, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5.
why: Effort is part of the cached prefix on most models.
check: Check whether the setup changes effort mid-task on models other than those listed, or runs on Bedrock/Vertex where the exception does not apply.
quote: on most models, each effort level has its own cache, so changing effort mid-session recomputes the entire request.

claim: Anthropic advises picking model and effort at the top of a session and saving /compact for natural breaks between tasks.
why: Fewer mid-task changes mean a higher cache hit rate.
check: Look for workflows that toggle model, effort or fast mode mid-task.
quote: Pick your model and effort level at the top of a session, then save `/compact` for natural breaks between tasks.

claim: Fast mode keeps a separate cache from standard speed, so it should be turned on at the start of a session; the first activation reads the whole conversation uncached at fast-mode rates.
why: Each speed toggle reads uncached whatever the other speed lacks.
check: Check for setups that toggle fast mode mid-session.
quote: To keep that cost small, turn it on at the start of a session.

claim: Tool definitions sit in the system-prompt layer, so adding or removing a tool definition invalidates the cache; with MCP tool search active (the default on supported models) the first request's tool list is kept all conversation and MCP connect/disconnect does not break the cache.
why: Deferred tools load on demand without changing the prefix.
check: If tool search is off or unavailable (some Vertex models, Foundry on Azure), check for mid-session MCP changes that invalidate the cache.
quote: Tool definitions sit in the system prompt layer, so the cache invalidates when the set of tool definitions in the request changes between turns.

claim: Plugin skills, commands, agents, hooks, monitors and themes never invalidate the cache; their content is appended after the existing conversation, while plugins providing MCP servers follow the MCP rules.
why: Appending leaves the prefix intact.
check: Enabling plugins mid-session is cheap unless they ship MCP servers.
quote: It appends their content after the existing conversation, so the next request pays for that content and still reads everything before it from the cache.

claim: Compaction by design invalidates the conversation layer, and project context (CLAUDE.md, auto memory, unscoped rules) is reloaded from disk and its cache rebuilt even when files are unchanged.
why: Project context is cached together with the conversation.
check: Count a compaction as a cache rebuild of the fixed context; large always-loaded instructions raise the cost of each compaction.
quote: It's cached together with the conversation, so after `/compact` or automatic compaction its cache is rebuilt even if its files are unchanged.

claim: A /compact while the cache is warm costs a fraction of what the context size suggests, but after a break longer than the cache lifetime the summarization request reprocesses the history uncached, making compaction most expensive when resuming an old session.
why: The summary request repeats the system prompt, tools and history.
check: Advise compacting at natural breaks while warm rather than after long idle gaps.
quote: there is no cache left to read, so the summarization request reprocesses that history as uncached input.

claim: To abandon a path entirely, /rewind to an earlier turn rather than compact, since rewind returns to an already cached prefix instead of building a new one.
why: The remaining history is the content the cache was built from.
check: Check whether users compact to recover from a bad path where /rewind would be cheaper.
quote: Rewinding truncates back to a prefix that is already cached, rather than building a new one as compaction does.

claim: Editing CLAUDE.md mid-session neither invalidates the cache nor takes effect; the new content loads on the next /clear, /compact or restart.
why: Project-root and user CLAUDE.md are read once at session start.
check: Do not credit mid-session edits for behavior change; require restart or /clear to test instruction edits.
quote: The new content loads on the next `/clear`, `/compact`, or restart.

claim: Skills, commands, plan mode, permission-mode changes, output-style changes and /recap all keep the cache because they append messages rather than change the prefix.
why: Content added in the conversation layer leaves the system prompt and project context cached.
check: These are cache-safe mid-session; only the exceptions (model-pinning skills, opusplan) cost a rebuild.
quote: These actions either append to the end of the conversation or don't touch the request at all.

claim: Removing old images or PDFs to stay under request limits rewrites the messages that held them, so the next request reprocesses the conversation from the earliest of those messages onward, one slow turn per batch.
why: Claude Code removes a batch of the oldest images at a time.
check: Screenshot-heavy sessions will see periodic uncached turns; suggest fresh sessions or fewer images.
quote: Removing images changes the messages that held them, so the next request reprocesses the conversation from the earliest of those messages onward.

claim: After a Claude Code upgrade the first conversation builds its cache from the top, because upgrades typically change the system prompt or tool definitions; auto-update applies only at next launch.
why: System prompt changes invalidate everything.
check: A setup that restarts and upgrades frequently pays an uncached first turn each time.
quote: A new Claude Code version typically updates the system prompt or tool definitions, so the first conversation you start after an upgrade builds its cache from the top.

claim: Cached prefixes expire after inactivity and each cache hit resets the timer; the API offers a 5-minute TTL and a 1-hour TTL, and the 1-hour TTL charges a higher cache write rate.
why: A longer TTL pays off only on idle-and-return use and costs more on short bursts.
check: Compare the user's typical idle gaps with the TTL their auth type gets.
quote: The time to live (TTL) controls how long a gap the cache survives. The API offers two: a five-minute TTL, and a

claim: By default the main conversation gets a one-hour TTL only on a Claude subscription within plan usage; with usage credits, an API key or a cloud provider it gets five minutes, and subagents, workflows, forks, compaction and titles get five minutes everywhere (except server-controlled helpers on subscription).
why: Claude Code drops to five minutes when usage is billed, since that has the lower write rate.
check: For API-key or cloud setups with idle gaps over five minutes, check whether promptCacheTtl is set to 1h.
quote: Unless you choose a TTL yourself, Claude Code requests the one-hour TTL only on a Claude subscription

claim: TTL is configurable per bucket (v2.1.242 or later) with promptCacheTtl or CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL for the main conversation and subagentPromptCacheTtl or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_PROMPT_CACHE_TTL for everything else; values are 5m or 1h, and FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M=1 overrides all.
why: Precedence runs FORCE_PROMPT_CACHING_5M, env var, setting, subagent cacheTtl frontmatter, ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H, then default.
check: Check settings and managed settings for TTL overrides that conflict with real idle patterns.
quote: Each control takes `5m` or `1h`, and Claude Code ignores any other value.

claim: A subagent's first request does not read the parent's cache because its system prompt and tools differ, whereas a fork inherits the parent's prefix and does read it.
why: Prefix match requires an identical prefix.
check: Each subagent type carries its own cache-warming cost; many distinct short-lived subagents multiply uncached input.
quote: so they get five minutes even on a subscription

claim: Claude Code's cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory, because the system prompt embeds auto memory paths and the conversation opens with working directory, platform, shell and OS.
why: Different directories build different prefixes.
check: Do not expect cache sharing across worktrees or directories.
quote: In Claude Code, the cache is effectively scoped to one machine and directory.

claim: Cache health is read from cache_read_input_tokens versus cache_creation_input_tokens in the status line current_usage object; a high read-to-creation ratio is good and creation staying high every turn means the prefix is changing.
why: The two counts are what the API reports per response.
check: Ask for a status line or /usage showing the ratio when diagnosing high cost.
quote: A high read-to-creation ratio means caching is working well. If creation stays high turn after turn, something is changing in your prefix.

claim: /usage adds a Prompt cache (main) line after the first response (v2.1.251 or later) showing request count, share of input tokens from cache, misses, expected rebuilds and warm/cold state; it covers the main conversation only, not subagents.
why: Misses and expected rebuilds (compaction, tool-result clearing) are counted separately.
check: Use /usage to see the cache hit share; subagent cache behavior needs OpenTelemetry instead.
quote: It covers the main conversation only, not subagents.

claim: To confirm which TTL cache writes used, read usage.cache_creation from claude -p output: ephemeral_1h_input_tokens for one-hour writes and ephemeral_5m_input_tokens for five-minute writes.
why: Claude Code reports writes split by TTL.
check: Use this to verify a promptCacheTtl override actually took effect.
quote: Claude Code reports one-hour cache writes under `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens` and five-minute cache writes under `ephemeral_5m_input_tokens`.

claim: Behind a gateway that strips cache_control markers while returning success, the entire conversation history bills as uncached input on every turn.
why: Whether caching works through a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL depends on the gateway.
check: For gateway setups, compare cache read tokens to expectations; zero reads suggest marker stripping.
quote: your entire conversation history bills as uncached input on every turn.

claim: Anthropic reports average Claude Code cost of about $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per month, with 90% of users under $30 per active day.
why: It is offered as a baseline for pilots.
check: Compare observed spend against this range before declaring a setup unusually expensive.
quote: Across enterprise deployments, the average cost is around \$13 per developer per active day and \$150-250 per developer per month

claim: The /usage Session block computes dollars locally from token counts at list price (unless a managed modelPricing table applies), so it is an estimate and not the bill; it resets on /clear.
why: Subscribers' usage is included in the plan, and contracted rates are not fetched.
check: Do not treat /usage dollar totals as authoritative billing.
quote: Claude Code computes the dollar figure locally from token counts at list price, unless a

claim: The /usage breakdown recommends a change for behaviors behind 10% or more of recent usage.
why: Shares show how much usage a row applies to, not how much would be saved, and can sum past 100%.
check: Use the attribution rows to rank which skills, MCP servers or CLAUDE.md files are worth their cost.
quote: Its breakdown recommends a change for behaviors behind 10% or more of your recent usage.

claim: /insights analyzes up to 200 unseen recent sessions on this machine into an HTML report at ~/.claude/usage-data/report.html, and its tokens count against plan or API usage.
why: It reports how you work (friction, suggestions) rather than token totals.
check: Use /insights for behavior patterns, /usage for token cost.
quote: A single run analyzes up to 200 sessions it hasn't seen before and skips very short ones.

claim: OpenTelemetry export works on every setup and is the only option that streams per-user token and cost metrics into your own stack in near real time; cloud-provider usage is not covered by Anthropic's analytics dashboards.
why: Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry billing lives in the cloud console.
check: For cloud-provider deployments, check that OTel or a gateway is configured if per-user cost is needed.
quote: works on every setup and is the only option that streams per-user token and cost metrics into your own observability stack in near real time.

claim: Claude Code OTel metrics claude_code.token.usage (types input, output, cacheRead, cacheCreation) and claude_code.cost.usage are incremented after each API request and can be segmented by model, skill.name, plugin.name, agent.name and query_source.
why: Attribution attributes let spend be assigned to specific skills, plugins or subagent types.
check: Use these attributes to find which skills, plugins or subagents drive spend; set OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1 to see real names rather than custom or third-party placeholders.
quote: Attributing spend to specific skills, plugins, or subagent types via the `skill.name`, `plugin.name`, and `agent.name` attributes

claim: In OTel data the input token count excludes cache reads and writes, which are reported separately, so total input is input plus cache_read plus cache_creation.
why: Claude Code exports the API usage block as is.
check: When computing a setup's input size from telemetry, add the three fields.
quote: so these values exclude tokens read from or written to the

claim: OTel cost figures are approximations; official billing data comes from the Console, org analytics or the cloud provider.
why: Cost is computed client-side from list prices.
check: Reconcile telemetry cost against the billing source before citing dollar savings.
quote: Cost metrics are approximations. For official billing data, see

claim: The claude_code.compaction event records trigger (auto or manual), duration, and approximate pre_tokens and post_tokens, and the api_request event carries cost_usd, token counts, cache_creation_5m and 1h counts and query_source such as compact.
why: These expose how often compaction runs and what it costs.
check: Use compaction events to see how large contexts get before compaction and how often auto-compaction fires.
quote: `pre_tokens`: Approximate token count before compaction

claim: Telemetry requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=1, and repository .claude/settings.json cannot turn it on or choose the endpoint; it must come from managed settings, shell or user settings.
why: It prevents a repo from capturing content or redirecting data.
check: If telemetry is expected but absent, check where the variables are set.
quote: Claude Code ignores the [OpenTelemetry exporter variables](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#variables-claude-code-ignores-in-env) in a repository's `.claude/settings.json` and `.claude/settings.local.json`, so a repository can't use them to turn telemetry on, choose where it goes, or capture content.

claim: MCP tool definitions are deferred by default so only names and server instructions enter context; CLI tools like gh, aws and gcloud are still more context-efficient than MCP servers, and unused servers should be disabled via /mcp.
why: CLI tools add no per-tool listing.
check: List configured MCP servers and flag unused ones or ones replaceable by a CLI.
quote: so only tool names and server instructions enter context until Claude uses a specific tool.

claim: Move workflow-specific instructions (PR reviews, migrations) out of CLAUDE.md into skills that load only on invocation, keeping CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.
why: CLAUDE.md tokens are present even during unrelated work.
check: Look for procedure-style sections in CLAUDE.md that apply to one task.
quote: those tokens are present even when

claim: Hooks can preprocess data so Claude sees only filtered output, such as grepping ERROR lines or tail -n 100 of test output, cutting context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds.
why: Large outputs otherwise enter the conversation and are resent every turn.
check: Look for repeated large tool outputs (test logs, builds) with no filtering hook.
quote: a hook can grep for `ERROR` and return only matching lines, reducing context from tens of thousands of tokens to hundreds.

claim: Verbose work such as tests, documentation fetches and log processing should be delegated to subagents so only a summary returns, though the subagent's own requests still use quota and can be put on a smaller model.
why: Output stays in the subagent's context window.
check: Check subagent model settings for cheap tasks; model: haiku is the example given.
quote: Running tests, fetching documentation, or processing log files can consume significant context.

claim: Sonnet handles most coding tasks and costs less than Opus; Opus is reserved for complex architecture or multi-step reasoning, and a switch to Opus also applies to subagents that inherit the session model.
why: Opus left as default is named a common cause of unexpectedly high spend.
check: Check the default model and whether subagents inherit an expensive one.
quote: Sonnet handles most coding tasks well and costs less than Opus.

claim: Extended thinking is on by default, billed as output tokens, with default budgets of tens of thousands of tokens per request on some models; thinking cannot be turned off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or Fable models, so effort is the lever there.
why: Thinking is a hidden output cost on simple tasks.
check: Check effort and MAX_THINKING_TOKENS settings against task difficulty.
quote: Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens, and the default budget can be tens of thousands of tokens per request depending on the model.

claim: Agent teams use about 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode, and each teammate loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills automatically.
why: Each teammate has its own context window.
check: If agent teams are enabled, check team size, teammate model (Sonnet suggested) and shutdown discipline.
quote: Agent teams use approximately 7x more tokens than standard sessions when teammates run in plan mode

claim: In a long session Claude Code sends the full conversation with every request and every tool-use round, so even a one-line question draws usage for the whole history at the cached rate, and the first message after a break longer than the cache lifetime reprocesses all context.
why: Long context, cache misses, scheduled tasks, subagents and compaction are the listed drivers of climbing usage.
check: Look for long-lived sessions, /loop tasks or idle-triggered activity.
quote: Claude Code sends your full conversation with every request, and each time Claude uses tools it sends another request carrying that batch of tool results.

claim: Session-scoped scheduled tasks fire on their interval even while the session is idle and send the full context each time.
why: Each firing is a new request carrying the whole conversation.
check: Check /loop and scheduled tasks on large-context sessions; /usage lists the heaviest loops.
quote: fires on its interval even while the session is idle, sending your full context each time

claim: Compacting a large context is itself a large request, whereas /clear costs nothing, so when continuity is not needed clearing is cheaper.
why: /compact reads the conversation it summarizes.
check: Prefer /clear between unrelated tasks in the recommendations.
quote: When you want a fresh start instead of continuity, `/clear` costs nothing

claim: Anthropic divides cost levers into free wins (prompt caching, token hygiene, prompt audit, batch) that do not touch quality, and tradeoffs (model choice, effort, output caps, budgets, multimodel) that exchange cost for intelligence.
why: Free wins go first because tradeoffs risk quality.
check: Check that a cost review exhausts free wins before recommending downgrades in model or effort.
quote: **Free wins** cut spend without touching quality: prompt caching, token hygiene, a prompt audit against the model you are running, and

claim: Anthropic's cost workflow orders levers: prompt caching first and always on, then input-token hygiene, loop hygiene, output tokens, batch, then effort and budgets, with model selection deliberately last; apply them in that order rather than by savings rank.
why: Tradeoffs change what the model can do and overshooting costs quality the free wins never touch.
check: Verify recommendations follow free wins, then effort/budgets, then model, one lever per change.
quote: (free wins -> effort/budgets -> model), not in savings-rank order

claim: Cost should be judged per completed task, not per token, since a pricier model that finishes in fewer turns can be cheaper and a cheap model that fails still bills its tokens plus retries.
why: Per-token lists do not predict the ranking.
check: Reject cost arguments based on sticker price alone.
quote: API spend is optimized in units of **cost per completed task, not cost per token**.

claim: Model choice comes after every other lever because it caps the intelligence ceiling; sweep effort on the current model first, check for an upgrade before a step-down, then move down one tier at a time against an eval.
why: Swapping models mid-conversation also cold-starts the cache.
check: Flag model downgrades proposed before effort and hygiene levers, or without an eval.
quote: Model choice constrains the intelligence ceiling, which is why it comes after every lever

claim: Without an eval, savings cannot be told apart from regressions, so tradeoff levers need an eval before applying while free wins are safe regardless.
why: Tradeoffs must be validated against pass rate.
check: Check whether the setup has an outcome check before endorsing effort or model reductions.
quote: without one, savings cannot be told apart from regressions.

claim: Tool search with deferred loading pays once tool schemas pass roughly 10K tokens, which MCP servers reach quickly; below that the search step is overhead.
why: Deferring small schema sets adds discovery turns for little saving.
check: Check total tool schema size before recommending deferral for small tool sets.
quote: Pays once schemas run past roughly 10K tokens (MCP servers reach that fast); below that the search step is overhead.

claim: Context editing and client-side pruning are context-window tools, not savings levers, because each clearing pass rewrites the cached conversation; clear in a few large batches.
why: In Anthropic's measurement context editing cost more than it saved on the short run.
check: Be skeptical of context-clearing features presented as cost savers in short sessions.
quote: **Context editing** (clearing old tool uses or thinking) **is a context-window tool, not a savings lever.**

claim: A subagent for self-contained bulky steps absorbs heavy tool results and returns one line, but it starts a fresh prefix with no cache shared with the parent.
why: Isolation saves context but forgoes the parent's cache.
check: Subagents help only when intermediate context is not needed by the deciding model.
quote: note the subagent starts a fresh prefix with no cache shared with the parent.

claim: Anthropic says prompt caching comes before any other cost lever because every agentic turn resends the whole growing conversation, so a 40-turn task cost grows roughly with the square of turn count.
why: Caching reprices the resend at roughly a tenth, a twentieth on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5.
check: Verify caching is active before reviewing anything else.
quote: A 40-turn task sends its first turn 40 times, so task cost grows with roughly the square of turn count.

claim: A healthy agent loop reads a median 84% of input from cache, with the top 10% at 94% or more; below about 80% something is probably breaking the cache.
why: Measured on a full day of real traffic.
check: Compare a setup's cache-read share against 80%.
quote: Below about 80%, look for something breaking the cache

claim: Anything that changes per request, such as a timestamp or queue position, must stay out of the stable prefix; a 25-token status line at the front of the system prompt made every request rewrite the whole conversation.
why: Placed at the end of the newest user turn it left the cache read intact.
check: Grep instruction and system prompt text for dates, IDs and dynamic values near the top.
quote: Put nothing that changes per request, such as a timestamp or a queue position, ahead of the stable prefix: it turns every request into a full cache write.

claim: Editing the system prompt cost about 25 to 50 times what the same text cost as a mid-conversation system message, and a top-level effort change cost 20 to 40 times a per-message change.
why: Edits to the prefix rewrite the cached conversation, which is billed at the write rate.
check: Where mid-conversation system messages are supported, check that changes use them rather than editing top-level system.
quote: Editing the system prompt cost about 25 to 50 times what the same text cost as a mid-conversation system message.

claim: The 1-hour cache writes at 2x input instead of 1.25x, and a miss on either duration bills the whole prefix at the write price; the 1-hour duration pays when about 1 turn in 20 follows a 5-minute-to-1-hour pause, and loses when gaps over an hour are common.
why: Break-even is about 1 turn in 30 on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.
check: Compare a setup's gap distribution with these rules before recommending a 1h TTL.
quote: A miss on either duration bills the whole prefix at the write price instead of the read price.

claim: Choose the cache duration when a conversation starts; adding a 1-hour entry to a 5-minute conversation rewrote the whole prompt once ($0.80 at 100,000 tokens on Opus 5.5 versus $0.02 for a cached read).
why: Mixing durations mid-conversation forces a rewrite.
check: Check for TTL changes mid-session.
quote: Choose the cache duration when a conversation starts.

claim: When a cache-invalidating change is needed, make it on the first request after a compaction, which cost least ($0.75 versus $0.92 at compaction and $0.95 mid-session on a triage agent).
why: The compaction-triggering request still carries the whole conversation.
check: Schedule tool or effort changes right after compaction.
quote: Making them on the next request, the first after the compaction, cost the least.

claim: In Anthropic's tool-search measurement, loading up to 502 tool definitions raised run cost from $0.55 to $1.02 while tool search kept it at $0.56 with similar accuracy.
why: Every attached tool definition is input on every turn.
check: Estimate token weight of MCP tool catalogs and recommend deferral when large.
quote: With tool search, the run cost stayed flat at every catalog size.

claim: Instructions written for older models can cost money on newer ones, because newer models follow them literally; removing verify twice cut Claude Opus 5 cost per ticket, with stale scaffolds also costing accuracy.
why: Over-obeyed text produces extra tool rounds and writing with no accuracy gain.
check: Scan instruction files for 'verify twice', 'be maximally thorough', mandatory procedures and scratchpads written for older models.
quote: A newer model follows such instructions to the letter, producing extra tool rounds and extra writing that you pay for with no gain in accuracy.

claim: Sweep effort on your own workload before adding a second model; medium effort cost about 59% as much as high on Sonnet 5.5 SWE-bench Pro for roughly 7 points lower score, and effort should be tested in separate sessions.
why: Changing effort mid-session invalidates the cache and distorts the comparison.
check: Ask for evidence of an effort sweep before approving multimodel setups.
quote: Sweep effort on your own workload before you add a second model.

claim: When outputs are checkable, run at low effort and re-run only failures at high; on Opus 5.5 SWE-bench Pro this solved about 97% at about $0.17 per task versus 95.3% at $0.29 all at high.
why: Failed cheap attempts are counted in the cost.
check: Applicable only with a reliable failure signal; it adds wall-clock latency on failures.
quote: run every task at a low setting and re-run only the failures at a higher one.

claim: Output tokens cost five times input tokens on Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1, and in an agent loop each output token returns as input on every later turn.
why: Long answers are paid for repeatedly.
check: Check for instructions that demand long reports or memos; a six-section memo cost about 2.5x a one-line answer at similar accuracy.
quote: Output tokens cost five times input tokens on Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.2, and Claude Fable 5.1, and in an agent loop every token the model writes comes back as input on every later turn

claim: For most agent workloads Anthropic recommends starting with Claude Opus 5.5 at its default medium effort, and reserving Fable 5.2 for demanding or long-horizon work; Haiku 5.5 suits high-volume work with checkable outputs.
why: On the SWE-bench Pro subset Opus 5.5 matched Fable 5.1 for about a fifth of the cost per solved task.
check: Compare a setup's default model with this starting point; this is dated advice tied to the current lineup.
quote: For most agent workloads, start with Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort (`medium`).

claim: Tune a single model before combining models; orchestrators beat the single model only on routine work with a long cost tail or work larger than one context window, and an advisor helps only if the executor actually consults it.
why: On dependent chains or work that fits one context the orchestrator's model alone at lower effort came out ahead.
check: Challenge multi-agent or advisor designs unless the work fans out beyond one context window.
quote: delegation came out ahead in only two situations

claim: Batch processing takes 50% off every token including cached ones for results within 24 hours, and is the second-largest free lever after caching for unattended work.
why: It trades latency for the discount and does not combine with fast mode.
check: Check scheduled or evaluation workloads for batch eligibility.
quote: The Batch API takes 50% off every token of a request, including cached ones, in exchange for results arriving any time within 24 hours.

claim: Prompt caching is a prefix match over tools, then system, then messages, so any change in the prefix invalidates everything after it; per-request values like timestamps, UUIDs, unsorted JSON or per-user tool lists silently break it.
why: Stable content must physically precede volatile content.
check: Grep prompt-building code for datetime.now, uuid, json.dumps without sort_keys and conditional system sections.
quote: Prompt caching is a prefix match. Any change anywhere in the prefix invalidates everything after it.**

claim: Cache lifetime is measured from the start of the request that writes or reads the entry, so generation time counts against it; a 5-minute entry breaks even after two requests and a 1-hour entry needs at least three.
why: Write costs 1.25x or 2x input, read about 0.1x on most models.
check: Slow generations near 5 minutes can lose the cache before the next request starts.
quote: The lifetime is measured from the **start** of the request that writes or reads the entry - generation time counts against it

claim: Caching regressions are silent (requests succeed, the bill rises), so verify cache_read_input_tokens after every prompt-assembly change and prefer a standing check; input_tokens is only the uncached remainder.
why: The usage fields are the only ground truth.
check: Ask whether any monitoring or test asserts cache reads above zero.
quote: The costliest caching failure in production is silent: requests keep succeeding, the bill is just higher - no error, nothing announces it.
